choices.text: Hold the 5:40 p.m. departure and ask the museum to guarantee release by 3:55 p.m. before the hold expires.
Present the 7:25 p.m. one-stop itinerary as the workable fallback and confirm the routing tradeoff before purchasing it.
Purchase the 7:25 p.m. one-stop itinerary because it is the most practical same-day option.
Present the 8:15 p.m. nonstop from the distant airport first, including the longer ground transfer and its $107 higher total cost.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: B and D are both feasible: B has simpler ground logistics and a lower total cost, while D preserves a direct flight at the price of a long transfer. The user's history resolves the decision by supporting a confirmed one-stop fallback when a suitable direct option is unavailable.
candidate.gold_action: Use the workable one-stop as the fallback, but obtain confirmation before booking it.
candidate.label_rationale: The nearby nonstop is not suitable because the museum release time makes its airport margin untenable. The history supports accepting a one-stop in this circumstance, but the St. Louis evidence records a trip-specific exception rather than blanket authority to book connections without confirmation.
candidate.query: A registrar must remain at a New Orleans museum until 4:30 p.m. Sunday, and the airport transfer reliably takes 45 minutes. The only 5:40 p.m. departure has no workable airport margin. A 7:25 p.m. itinerary gets home that night, while an 8:15 p.m. departure from an airport 95 minutes away also remains feasible. No flight has been approved yet. What should the planner do next?

choices.text: Lead with the $361 nonstop arriving at 10:05 p.m., and retain the less expensive connection as an alternative.
Lead with a $329 itinerary connecting in Denver and arriving at 7:50 p.m., since it splits the difference on fare and arrival.
Lead with the $282 one-stop arriving at 8:45 p.m., since this work leg does not originate at the traveler's home airport.
Lead with a $344 flight to Dayton arriving at 8:10 p.m., followed by a 65-minute car transfer to Cincinnati.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: C is cheaper and arrives earlier, while A avoids a connection. The unusual trip origin makes overfitting to prior routes tempting, so selecting A requires abstracting the true scope from the evidence rather than matching surface details.
candidate.gold_action: Apply the museum-work routing preference to the direct-from-leisure-origin work leg and lead with the nonstop.
candidate.label_rationale: The durable scope is defined by the purpose and fixed museum access window, not by departure from the traveler's home city. A is therefore the correct transfer of the policy; C is a near miss that improperly narrows the pattern to the origins seen in prior episodes.
candidate.query: The traveler will finish a personal weekend in Seattle and then fly directly to a Monday museum condition review in Cincinnati, rather than beginning the work trip from home. Both leading options arrive Sunday night with ample time before the 8:30 a.m. access window. What should the planner lead with?

choices.text: Propose a $242 nonstop the next morning and add one hotel night, producing the lowest airfare but delaying the return.
Propose the $335 nonstop departing at 7:20 p.m. and arriving at 10:55 p.m.
Propose a $301 one-stop departing at 6:35 p.m. and arriving at 11:05 p.m., saving $34 with nearly the same arrival.
Propose the $260 one-stop departing at 5:45 p.m. and arriving at 10:15 p.m., which is cheaper and gets home earlier.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: The gold does not dominate: D improves both price and arrival time, while B alone offers routing simplicity. The prior return-flight evidence is necessary to know that this user has previously chosen the latter tradeoff in the same work context.
candidate.gold_action: Propose the same-evening nonstop return first.
candidate.label_rationale: The established preference covers return flights on fixed-schedule museum trips. B is suitable and should lead even though D is cheaper and arrives earlier; the policy is a preference, so D can still be shown as an alternative.
candidate.query: A museum installation in Minneapolis is scheduled to release the traveler at 3:30 p.m. Thursday, with a reliable 40-minute ride to the airport. Both main return options provide acceptable airport margins and arrive in Charlotte that night. Which return should be proposed first?

choices.text: Lead with the $248 one-stop arriving at 6:20 p.m., treating the earlier connected return as the user's updated routing norm.
Lead with a $292 one-stop arriving at 5:35 p.m., but note that its longer connection provides more disruption recovery time.
Lead with the $326 nonstop arriving at 7:10 p.m., treating the earlier connected return as a trip-specific exception.
Lead with a $304 flight to Toledo arriving at 6:00 p.m., followed by a 60-minute car transfer to Detroit.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: A is less expensive and arrives earlier, and it can be made to look historically supported by overgeneralizing a real prior choice. Correctly selecting C requires distinguishing an approved one-trip exception from a permanent preference revision.
candidate.gold_action: Return to the established default for the new trip and treat the prior one-stop as a limited exception.
candidate.label_rationale: Session s0046 supports one connected return only after the workable direct economy option was lost; it does not revise the recurring policy. The later support evidence confirms that suitable direct service should again lead on a new fixed-window museum trip.
candidate.query: For a new Detroit museum loan inspection, suitable economy seats are available on both a direct itinerary and a connecting itinerary. The travel record also contains one earlier museum return that used a connection after the workable direct economy inventory disappeared. How should that record affect the new shortlist?

leakage_signals: The prior-trip explanation is an explicit wording cue that identifies the connected itinerary as an exception; no private history beyond the query is needed.
query_only_verdict.rationale: The query explicitly says the earlier connected trip occurred only after workable direct economy inventory disappeared. That is trip-specific evidence and does not establish a new preference for connections, so the available nonstop should lead.

choices.text: Ask the museum to release the registrar early enough for the Sunday nonstop, and keep that flight on hold while awaiting an answer.
Present the Sunday one-stop as the workable same-night fallback, compare it with the overnight nonstop plan, and obtain the registrar's confirmation before purchasing the connection.
Submit the Sunday one-stop for immediate ticketing because it avoids the hotel night and returns the registrar home that evening.
Lead with the next-morning nonstop and hotel package because its routing is simpler, while listing the Sunday connection as the alternate.

candidate.difficulty_rationale: B and D preserve different benefits: B is less expensive and returns the registrar Sunday night, while D retains nonstop routing and requires an extra night. The stated constraints do not determine whether same-night arrival or routing simplicity matters more; the longitudinal evidence is needed to know that a one-stop may be used as a confirmed fallback when the workable nonstop schedule fails.
candidate.gold_action: Use the workable one-stop as the same-night fallback, while confirming the routing tradeoff before purchase.
candidate.label_rationale: Session s0031 establishes that a connection may remain in reserve when the nonstop schedule fails, s0046 shows that the traveler has accepted a one-stop return when the workable nonstop was unavailable, and s0068 confirms that nonstop routing remains the usual choice rather than an absolute rule. Here there is no workable Sunday nonstop, so the connected itinerary can be advanced as the same-night fallback, but the trip-specific exception evidence does not authorize purchasing it without confirmation.
candidate.query: A registrar will finish work at a New Orleans museum at 4:30 p.m. Sunday, followed by a reliable 45-minute ride to the nearby airport. The last departure that could get the registrar home without a connection leaves too early to provide a workable airport margin. A $386 one-stop departs at 7:25 p.m. and arrives at 11:40 p.m.; a next-morning nonstop would require a $184 hotel night but would arrive by 9:05 a.m. Monday. The registrar has no Monday-morning obligation, and nothing has been approved. What should the planner do next?

leakage_signals: The phrases 'nothing has been approved' and 'What should the planner do next?' cue a confirmation-before-purchase workflow.
The explicit statement that the last Sunday nonstop leaves too early rules out treating it as a currently workable itinerary.
query_only_verdict.rationale: The Sunday nonstop is infeasible under the stated work-release time and airport margin. Because nothing has been approved and there is no Monday-morning obligation, the planner should compare the feasible same-night connection with the overnight nonstop and obtain confirmation before purchasing. Immediate ticketing or privileging either feasible option without confirmation is not justified.
